changes.after: Make a table heading cover more than one row or column.

before: A spanning cell covers several grid positions. It does not, by that fact alone, explain every data cell’s headers. For this small two-level table, explicitly name each relevant header rather than relying on visual alignment.

colspan="2" makes Spring occupy two columns; rowspan="2" makes Room occupy two header rows. A th id names one header uniquely. A td headers attribute is a space-separated list of those header IDs: not visible labels and not CSS selectors. This example uses explicit headers relationships rather than mixing in an unexplained scope="colgroup" strategy.

```html
Workshop bookings
RoomSpring
MayJune
Studio85
``` The 8 cell names Studio, Spring and May through studio season may. The 5 cell names Studio, Spring and June. The May and June cells occupy the two positions beneath Spring; Room already occupies the first position in both header rows. Keep tables as simple as the data permits, and test complex relationships with assistive technology.

Build this three-column bookings table. Keep the two spans, unique header IDs and explicit headers lists on both data cells. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.
after: A table cell can cover more than one space. `colspan` makes it span columns across the table. `rowspan` makes it span rows down the table.
When a table has several levels of headings, tell each value which headings describe it. Give each `<th>` a unique id. On a `<td>`, use `headers` to list those ids with spaces between them.

This table groups May and June under Spring. ```html
Workshop bookings
RoomSpring
MayJune
Studio85
``` Spring spans two columns. Room spans two header rows. The value `8` lists `studio season may`, so its labels are Studio, Spring and May. The value `5` uses June instead.

Build the shown bookings table. Keep Room’s rowspan and Spring’s colspan at 2. Give every header its shown id. Set the first data cell’s headers to `studio season may` and the second to `studio season june`. Run the checks and make sure each value points to the right month.

before.question: The 8 cell’s headers changes to "studio season june", but the cell stays visually under May. Is its explicit month relationship still correct?
choices: Yes, visual placement overrides the headers list.
No. It now explicitly references June, despite its unchanged position.
before.explanation: The headers tokens identify header elements. Valid IDs can still express the wrong relationship; existence checks alone cannot judge meaning.

after.question: The value under May has headers="studio season june". Is its month label correct?
choices: Yes. Its position overrides the list.
No. The list points to June.
after.explanation: The headers list names the connected headings. It must match the meaning of the value, not just contain real ids.
